sections.b: Twenty-one verses: a sentence against Edom (1-9), the charge of violence against a brother (10-14), the day of the LORD for all nations (15-16), and Zion's restoration (17-21). It is the shortest book in the Old Testament and the only one with a single target. The first nine verses echo Jeremiah 49:7-22.

common: Most scholars date the charge in verses 10-14 to the years after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
uncommon: A minority dates the book to the 800s BC, under Jehoram.

claude.title: Brought down, then going up
claude.body: The book is framed by a reversal of height: Edom is brought down (verses 3-4) and rescuers go up Zion (verse 21).

sections.b: Obadiah is the Bible's sharpest word against Edom. It promises to bring Edom down from its rock strongholds (verses 1-4), says its allies will betray it (verse 7) and charges it with standing aside, gloating, looting and cutting off refugees on the day Jerusalem fell (verses 10-14). The ground is kinship: Edom is Jacob's "brother." Verses 18-19 say the house of Esau will be stubble and that the people of the Negev will take over Mount Esau. In the centuries after, Edomites moved into southern Judea as Idumeans, so the promise has been read as a vivid exaggeration (as Malachi 1:2-5 suggests), as a judgment on the kingdom only, or as a statement about all God's enemies. Verses 1-9 closely resemble Jeremiah 49:7-22.
sections.refs: Obadiah 1:1-4; Obadiah 1:7; Obadiah 1:10-14; Obadiah 1:18-19; Jeremiah 49:7-22; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 35:1-15; Malachi 1:2-5

sections.b: After about 550 BC Arab tribes pressed into Edom's land, and Edomites moved into the Negev and the south of Judea, a region later called Idumea. The Nabataeans, an Arab people, built Petra and took over the old Edomite heartland. Judas Maccabeus fought Idumeans (1 Maccabees 5:3, 65), and John Hyrcanus conquered them about 125 BC and forced them to be circumcised (Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1). Herod the Great was of Idumean descent. Obadiah does not mention any of this and does not predict Herod.

common: Obadiah's charge against Edom is dated by most scholars to the aftermath of 586 BC.
uncommon: Some date Obadiah 10-14 to the 800s BC, under Jehoram.

claude.title: Why Edom, of all nations
claude.body: Obadiah's anger is sharper than at Babylon, which does not appear in the book. My reading is that the hurt of betrayal by kin is the reason: an enemy is expected to attack; a brother is expected to help. This overlaps with the common observation that the charge depends on the brother theme.

sections.h: Obadiah: the day of the LORD against all the nations
sections.b: Obadiah uses "day" ten times for the day Jerusalem fell (verses 11-14), and then declares that "the day of the LORD is near, against all the nations" (verse 15). The phrase turns a judgment on one nation, Edom, into a rule for all: it will be done to you just as you did it. The day brings both judgment (verses 15-16) and the rescue of Zion's survivors (verses 17-21). The sequence matches Joel, which comes two books earlier in the Hebrew order of the Twelve.
sections.refs: Obadiah 1:8; Obadiah 1:11-15; Joel 1:15; Joel 3:14; Isaiah 13:6; Ezekiel 30:3; Amos 5:18-20

sections.h: Obadiah 15: it will be done to you
sections.b: "It will be done to you just as you did it. Your payback will return on your own head." Obadiah states the rule that the punishment fits the crime. Edom gloated, took part in looting and handed over survivors, and the same will be done to it. The rule is not limited to Edom: it comes with the day of the LORD "against all the nations." Joel 3:4, 7 uses the same Hebrew phrase of Tyre, Sidon and Philistia; Habakkuk 2:8, 16 says it of Babylon. The New Testament repeats the principle in Matthew 7:2, Galatians 6:7 and Revelation 18:6. Churches differ on how believers should hear it (see the card at Obadiah 15).
sections.refs: Obadiah 1:15; Joel 3:4; Habakkuk 2:8; Habakkuk 2:16; Psalm 137:8; Matthew 7:2; Galatians 6:7; Revelation 18:6

sections.b: In Obadiah "Jacob" is the nation, set against Esau (verses 10, 17, 18). Verse 12 names Judah, the people whose city fell, and verse 18 names Joseph, the northern tribes, so that the fire and flame that burn Esau come from the whole house of Jacob, south and north together, as in Ezekiel 37:15-22.

Verse 16 calls Zion "my holy mountain" where the people drank the cup of judgment, and verses 17 and 21 give it a future: survivors, holiness, and rescuers going up to judge Mount Esau, with royal power the LORD's. Verse 17 is close to Joel 2:32. The contrast with Mount Esau runs through the end of the book.

The word is peletah, "survivors, those who escape" (verse 17), the same word as in Joel 2:32. Edom is told that no survivor will be left to its house (verse 18); Zion is promised survivors. The remnant here is a group that makes it through the day of the LORD, not just a leftover.

sections.h: Obadiah: the exiles of Jerusalem and the northern tribes
sections.b: Verse 20 speaks of the exiles of "this army of Israelites," who are to take the land as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem "in Sepharad," who are to take the cities of the Negev. Where Sepharad is (Sardis, or another place) is debated; the later reading of it as Spain comes from the Aramaic Targum and is reception. The verse shows a Jewish community already scattered far across the Persian world.

Obadiah 11 describes foreigners entering Jerusalem's gates and casting lots for it. Verses 12-14 name the people of Judah and "my people" as those harmed. The fall of the city is the day to which the whole book looks back; the Hebrew text keeps repeating "the day of" it.

sections.h: Obadiah: Edom on the day of the fall
sections.b: Obadiah 10-14 charges Edom with standing aside, entering the city's gate, looting and holding the crossroads where refugees fled, on the day Jerusalem fell. Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 25:12-14 and 35 make the same charge. Jeremiah 40:11 shows other Judeans fleeing to Edom and returning, so Edom's behavior may have been mixed. The Bible's accounts of the fall (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 39; 52) do not mention Edom, and nothing outside the Bible records its part in detail.
sections.refs: Obadiah 1:10-14; 2 Kings 25:8-11; Jeremiah 40:11; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 25:12-14; Ezekiel 35:5-15

sections.b: "You drank on my holy mountain. So all the nations will drink and drink." The cup is the cup of the LORD's anger, which Judah drank in the fall of Jerusalem and which the nations will now drink. The "you" is plural, so the verse is not about Edom alone. Readers also take it of the carousing of Jerusalem's enemies on the temple hill. Compare Jeremiah 25:15-29, Isaiah 51:17-23, Lamentations 4:21 and Habakkuk 2:16.
sections.refs: Obadiah 1:16; Jeremiah 25:15-29; Jeremiah 49:12; Isaiah 51:17-23; Lamentations 4:21; Psalm 75:8; Habakkuk 2:16

sections.b: Verse 16 pictures the nations drinking the LORD's cup until they are as if they had never been. The cup of wrath passes from Judah to the nations, and Lamentations 4:21 says it will also pass to Edom.

Obadiah is a whole book that is one oracle against a nation. It opens like Jeremiah 49:7-22 with a call to the nations to rise against Edom (verse 1), gives the charge in verses 10-14, then turns to "all the nations" and the day of the LORD (verse 15). Like other oracles against nations, it was most likely addressed to Judah, not delivered in Edom. The rhetoric of address, "you," makes the point for Judah's survivors.
sections.refs: Obadiah 1:1; Obadiah 1:10-15; Jeremiah 49:7-22; Amos 1:11-12; Ezekiel 25:12-14; Ezekiel 35

sections.b: Edom and Esau became loaded labels. In rabbinic writing Edom stands for Rome and later the Christian world. In some Christian interpretation, Genesis 25:23 ("the elder will serve the younger") was read of the Jews and the church (already in Augustine, City of God 16.35), and the language of Esau and Edom was later used in anti-Jewish polemic. Obadiah's "house of Esau" was caught up in that use. Neither use is in Obadiah, whose Edom is a real nation that betrayed its kin. Readers should keep Obadiah's own target in view and not turn "Edom" into a label for any people today.

sections.h: Obadiah 17-21: Zion, Jacob and the land
sections.b: Verses 17-21 promise survivors on Zion, a Jacob that burns like fire and takes back its lands, and rescuers on Zion. Churches differ on who these are: the Jewish people in their land, the church as the new Israel, or both in different ways. See the card at Obadiah 17-21.

sections.h: Esau and Edom as a type
sections.b: Obadiah's Edom is a real nation. Later readers also treated Esau as a figure: of those who oppose the people of God (Jerome's line), of the world, or of the unrepentant heart. Paul uses Jacob and Esau in Romans 9:10-13. Churches differ on whether an Old Testament nation can carry more than one sense (see the card at Obadiah).

sections.h: Obadiah 19-20: the map of recovered lands
sections.b: The Negev, the Shephelah, Ephraim and Samaria, Gilead, Zarephath and Sepharad: Obadiah lists lands the restored people will take over, on all sides of Judah. The lists do not match any known conquest, and the verb yarash, "take over," repeats four times in verses 17-20.

Verse 19 says the people of the Shephelah, the foothills, will take over the Philistines' land. By the time Obadiah's verses were written the Philistine cities had been ruined by Babylon, so the line speaks of the old coastal plain as a land to be reclaimed.

sections.h: Obadiah 21: royal power will belong to the LORD
sections.b: The last line of Obadiah says the LORD will have the royal power (hamelukhah). The word is the one in Psalm 22:28. The line brings the whole book to its end: Edom's fall and Judah's recovery serve the LORD's rule. Zechariah 14:9, Daniel 7:27 and Revelation 11:15 say the same.

Obadiah 5 argues that even grape harvesters leave a few gleanings. The law told Israelites to leave them for the poor (Leviticus 19:10; Deuteronomy 24:21), so the picture is of harvesters who keep the rule. Edom's destroyers will not.
Foreigners "cast lots for Jerusalem": conquerors divided captives and spoil by lot. Joel 3:3 and Nahum 3:10 use the same picture.
